utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, we are awaiting the arrival of the accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before I continue, I have the impression, Mr. May, that you didn't bear in mind that we were rather late starting on Friday as well due to transportation problems. So I would kindly ask you to consider giving me a little more time tomorrow, because we were half an hour late on Friday, and now we're again ten minutes late. And also, Mr. Nice spent some time on Friday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We have in mind the times which have been lost in your cross-examination. I don't know why we were late today. We should have started on time. But we will make some inquiries about that. But any delay is noted. However, we will consider whether you should have more time. It will partly depend -- you asked for a little more time tomorrow. That will partly depend on how we get on today and whether any time is wasted or not in cross-examination. Now, let us begin.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I hope we will be efficiently using the time available and as rationally as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So let us now make an excursion to your first information about the crimes in Kosovo that you testified about mostly. You testified here that you first learnt about that sometime in May. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You informed the Chief of the Supreme Command, General Ojdanic, about what you had learnt; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you have your notes on you, those that I saw you using?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't use any notes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm talking about the notes you used, your notes that you used when you were making the statement to the investigators.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have them on me, but I know what is written in them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that in your notes it says that General Ojdanic, on that occasion, explicitly stated his own position as well as the position of the Supreme Staff and the Supreme Commander - that is my position - emphasising both, that crimes committed may not be concealed and that the perpetrators have to be punished?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Ojdanic didn't say that. My notes say that you said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But he also said that. Before the meeting with me, he had conveyed my position to you; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. On the 16th of May, in the evening, he said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I have a tape here which can be played if there is something you do not remember.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember everything. There is no problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So there's no dispute that as soon as you learnt about the crimes, my position was conveyed to you, the position of the Supreme Command, the position of the Chief of Staff of the Supreme Command, that crimes may not be concealed and that the perpetrators must all be punished.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that the Chief of Staff at the time, General Ojdanic, ordered also that General Pavkovic, the commander of the 3rd Army now, should come to Belgrade to report about the information that your organs had collected?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it also true that on that occasion Ojdanic ordered you and Pavkovic to collect the relevant documentation about the crimes and that he said that a joint meeting had been scheduled with the civilian security service?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was after the meeting. At the meeting on the 17th of May, you gave the task that the two services, the military and state security services, must not clash amongst themselves, that it was in the interest of the nation that they cooperate, and this was at the meeting of the 17th of May. We did not discuss that on the 16th of May or the 13th of May. At the meeting on the 17th of May, you gave instructions that the top leadership of both services should meet and resolve any problems they may have.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So that was my reaction having heard of the problems that the military and the civilian, that is the army and the police, are shifting the blame from one to the other?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did I say then that the state may not tolerate a single crime?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You said that major crimes must necessarily be addressed and sanctioned and that the state may not allow the two services to clash amongst themselves, and that you wished to be informed about any problem that may arise in that cooperation and that whoever obstructs that cooperation, he was harming the interests of the state. And you used the expression that that was equal to sabotage.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. And I insisted that the bodies whose duty it was should cooperate amongst themselves on both the military and the civilian sides and that nothing may remain hidden or concealed; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. We'll be saving time now. Is it true -- maybe we'll save time regarding the tapes -- that according to Pavkovic's reports, 271 persons were registered as killed as the responsibility of the army, 326 for which the MUP was responsible, which makes a total of over 600.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Were the figures given by the MUP higher than those given by the army? Was the number given by the MUP larger than that given by the army?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to information conveyed by General Pavkovic on the 16th of May at the preparatory meeting for the meeting with you, it was stated that the MUP was accusing the army of being responsible for almost 800 deaths. And then there was some coordination, 271 and 326. So this amounted to less than 800.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But MUP gave its estimates, its figures, the figures it had available to it, according to which those figures were higher than the ones presented by the army.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Does that imply that MUP was not concealing figures when it gave a figure that was higher than the one you had?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It depends who the figures are being hidden from. If we're talking about the army, I assume they were not concealing it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It's not a question of the army, but it was a joint meeting of the civilian and military bodies. You told us who attended the meeting. There was the top military leadership, the Chief of the Main Staff, the staff of the Supreme Command, you as the person reporting.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The coordination of the figures, that is 271 and 326, was not done at the meeting you attended.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Of course not. You submitted a report on the details at the meeting with me and what it was all about. But before that, you coordinated your figures with the police.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was probably done by General Pavkovic over there in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In any event, the figures agreed on indicated that the number was higher for which the police was responsible. Can we infer from that that the police was not seeking to conceal any crime committed by anyone for whom they were responsible?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot give judgements as to what they thought. I gave the facts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So that is a fact, that they presented a higher number. Is it true, according to your knowledge and according to what your services were responsible for, the military security services, the civilian security services, the military prosecutors and civilian prosecutors, the military judiciary and civilian judiciary; isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What for?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: For the prosecution of these crimes. So did the bodies, as far as you knew - I'm referring to the military security - take every possible measure for all the acts to be discovered and the perpetrators taken to court?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as the military organs are concerned, yes. Even upon the completion of military operations, one person was found and arrested who was in hiding, and he was found on the 26th of June in Valjevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In addition to what I have already emphasised, that not a single crime may be concealed, that I emphasised and named the entire top leadership of the Ministry of the Interior and said that not any one of them had any reason to protect anyone, because there was reference to certain paramilitary formations that had or, rather, whose members had committed certain crimes. Is that what is stated in your notes?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is not only stated in my notes but that is how it was. That is what you told Rade Markovic to pass on to Rodja and Vlajko, you said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And I said that nobody would have any reason to protect anyone?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but that their heads would not roll.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but they must be held responsible?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they must be held responsible.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So can we say then that these were individual perpetrators of crimes and not something for which any, I would call it, institution can be blamed within the chain of command?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to my knowledge and on the basis of that meeting, that could be only partially true, because at that meeting we reported about a group, saying that after having committed a crime in Podujevo, instead of being arrested, they were returned to Gnjilane where again they committed a crime.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did I say in response to that that that group must be held responsible?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you did, but your question was not that. Your question was in the chain of command.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, precisely. In the chain of command, did anyone order something to be committed that could be called a crime? As for this group - I won't mention the names because you don't wish the names to be mentioned in public session - didn't I say with respect to that group that the persons that you reported had committed a crime had to be held responsible? Is that what I said?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did I point out on that occasion precisely because of this matter of the shifting of the blame from one to the other that both services have to work for the state and not for anyone else and that they have to cooperate amongst themselves in state affairs and that the state must not, may not tolerate a single crime? I was very categorical about that, wasn't I?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You said that we respect to the cooperation between the services, and you said that major crimes have to be resolved, that the state would not tolerate them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I said all drastic acts have to be resolved, and every crime is a drastic act. There is no rape that is a minor crime or a killing that's a minor crime. But every drastic act had to be resolved. Is that what I said?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what you said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember well this meeting - because you also mentioned this group which you said had committed crimes and I said that they must be taken to task - did I say that you had to check whether there was any other paramilitary formation in Kosovo that might crop up a week later with a new crime? Did I say that?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that from the very outset the presence of any paramilitary formations was absolutely prohibited and that the commanders had strict orders to disarm any paramilitary formation immediately and to arrest them?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am aware of that order regarding the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, you're a general, so you have to know about that. After all, you spoke about the order of the Supreme Command given to strategic groups in the form of a directive; isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that that directive contains the obligation and duty strictly to respect the law of war, to take care of prisoners of war, and especially of the civilian population and all these other matters that we're mentioning now and which this fake indictment is charging me with?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was even a small memo given to each member of the army to use, even myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So there was even a memo reminding people of the obligation to respect civil rights and so on, and to protect the civilian population and so on; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Since you headed the intelligence -- no, sorry, the security administration, do you remember their - and when I say "their" I'm talking about the KLA - notes which your bodies managed to get hold of and from which it is evident that at the moment NATO attacks Yugoslavia, the army and the police has to be attacked and the civilian population should be pulled out, as they say, to safer regions, and that is Macedonia, Albania, and Montenegro. That can be found in their diaries.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that -- I don't know that. Probably because I was not in active service at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know that the scenario was to chase the civilians out of Kosovo, and that was the scenario on the basis of which we were accused of deportation of Albanians from Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know, since you headed the security department, that anybody at any level, even at the municipal level, ordered the deportation of Albanians out of Kosovo, forcing them out of Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not aware of any such orders, but I know of the case that I mentioned in Kaludjerski Laz, that a group, Kaludjerski Laz, that a group was chased to Rozaje municipality and executed there. I testified about that case.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But that is one of the crimes that I said the perpetrators of which had to be taken to court. So there's no dispute over that. My question is whether anyone --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let us have the answer recorded. This crime to do with Rozaje, the accused suggests it's one of the crimes that he said the perpetrators had to be taken to court. Is that right or not, General?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said what this was all about during my previous testimony. I also mentioned the name of the person who took part in that group that was chasing this group of Albanians. I mentioned the example of two women and little girls that had been wounded and had put up by the military police into a hospital. And they also carried out an investigation, however, what was ultimately done is something I don't know. This is information I got while I was still not in active service. It was on the 23rd and 24th of April. And also I presented an example from Mitrovica and how certain groups behaved there towards civilians. But I don't know about any position or order to do so. I just know that things like that did happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The position and the order was that such cases should be arrested and brought before a court of law.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that such an order was issued for sure in the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And whose position could it have been that little girls should be killed and that people should be chased to Rozaje, et cetera, except for some criminal? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what was done. I can give a wider answer to that now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Please let's just not waste any time. Please.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All right. I'll give brief answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Please. You were staying in Kosovo on the 2nd of June precisely because of crimes that had been committed?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You were there from the 2nd until the 7th?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was there from the 1st until the 7th.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Precisely because of these crimes that we discussed at that meeting on the 15th of May?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It was not only due to the crimes but this was an all-around tour of the security organs and also to look into the question of crimes in greater detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Please. Is it true that you managed to record then when you were there everything; killings, liquidations, rapes, lootings, especially what was done by individuals from the ranks the army?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not everything; some characteristic cases about which the organs I toured informed me of.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, did you ascertain anywhere that anyone, even the lowest-ranking commander, commander of a company or whatever, did any commander ever issue an order to have a crime committed, or were these arbitrarily committed crimes by individuals? Did you establish that any commander at any level, of the lowest ranking unit, had ever issued an order to commit a crime?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no information that anybody had issued this kind of order. There were two cases where there was a tolerant attitude towards those who had committed that arbitrarily.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Those who had this tolerant position, were they also held accountable?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Let's move on then. Let's move on then. Is it correct that for the most part the crimes that you investigated, that is to say where the members of the military were considered to be responsible, were primarily perpetrated by reservists or volunteers who were included in the units? There was a vast number of people, and among them certainly there were such individuals as well. Is this the predominant characteristic, that these were primarily reservists or volunteers?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you remember that the main criterion when volunteers were taken in was supposed to be their - how should I put this? - psychological stability and only then establishing whether they were physically fit? Of course they'd have to be physically fit, but emphasis was laid on the fact that people who were unstable and who had frayed nerves should not be taken into the units; they might violate the law.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and a selection was made. Fifty per cent were taken in.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Oh. That means that 50 per cent of those who had volunteered were rejected?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. We don't have time to deal with these matters any longer. We've saved time because we don't have to play the tapes. So now I'm going to go back to where we had left off. Is it correct -- I'm going back to Vukovar now, General. Is it correct that crimes, at least according to what we know, in that area were primarily committed by local criminals?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether they were local or whether they had been criminals before that, because the Dusan Silni detachment that I mentioned was not from that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: We established the origins of that, and I don't think that there was any controversy involved. And is it correct that in 1998, you had a meeting with Sljivancanin, an encounter with Sljivancanin, and is it correct that on that occasion he said to you that he had had a clash with local civilians who wanted to kill him as well because he protected prisoners? And when he started taking them out and treating them in accordance with the rules of service, I mean the prisoners, and that therefore, they had to provide security for these prisoners so that nothing would happen to them. Is that right or is that not right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This conversation that I had with him took place in 1997, and you interpreted it correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did he also tell you that when some of the prisoners at the barracks in Vukovar were set free, these same civilians or territorials broke into the barracks and therefore the army had to transport civilians to a safer place precisely in order to save them from the enraged territorials who reacted to the crimes that had been committed before that?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did he act as an honourable man, believing that the crimes that they had committed cannot be a justification for any other crime? One crime cannot be justified for by another?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, just a moment. It's not for the witness to say whether Sljivancanin behaved in an honourable way or not. All he can tell us is what Sljivancanin himself said. It's not for the witness to say whether it was an honourable action or not. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Please. After that, the only competent organs in the territory, were they the organs of the SAO Krajina? After the fall of Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. This organisation of government, the way it was. However, since the army remained there, then I know that later on military commands were established of particular towns. That is to say that the position was that there was a civilian government as the executive government, but then there were also military organs for a while.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When you say "military," you are not actually referring to the JNA, you are referring to the local Territorial Defence, aren't you? Is that right or is that not right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Until the end of 1991, I think there were still town commands in place.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, you say that you first heard of the Ovcara case from a person whose last name is Muris, who was commander of the anti-terrorist platoon; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: However, he was not at Ovcara as far as I managed to understand your explanation. Did I understand you properly or not? Did I understand your explanation properly or not?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to what he said to me, he had been sent to go to Ovcara because it was known that there were some problems there. And when he got close to Ovcara, he heard gunshots and informed the command about that. How far he got, whether he got to the area where the prisoners were, or close to that area, is something that I don't know. He said quite literally, "When I got to Ovcara, I heard gunshots and I reported about that."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But he did not know who was going on there. He could not establish what was going on there.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not then. Later on, he found out too.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Later on, like you, he only could have found out from someone who perhaps could have been a direct witness, but he had not been there; is that right? But is it correct that as for all your further knowledge, you obtained that when talking to, if I understood your statement correctly, the journalist Jovan Dulovic first, and he said Radic, Mrksic, or Sljivancanin had nothing to do with what was going on at Ovcara; is that right or is that not right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not only through him. There are several persons. I made a statement before the military court, and I mentioned all these persons in succession as to what I heard from whom. However, most of the details in the first stage I got from these journalists, and it is correct that they said to me what you mentioned just now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. In addition to what you heard from him, because he's independent, he's a journalist, he has nothing to do with the crimes, except for what you heard from him, what you compiled later as information, did that precisely corroborate what he had told you about and what others said, that Radic, Mrksic, and Sljivancanin had nothing to do with what had happened in Ovcara; is that right or is that not right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And did you come to learn that the JNA had anything to do with what happened at Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It did have something to do with it because these prisoners were practically, at that time, under the control of the JNA, under the control of the 80th Motorised Brigade in whose area this area where they were guarded was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Are you trying to say the area of responsibility of that brigade?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Within the deployed area where that brigade was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: However, as far as I managed to understand, it is precisely some people that you had talked to who told you about what had happened there and that actually the army had nothing to do with it. Is that right or is that not right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He just answered that question. He's given you the answer: Because the prisoners were practically under the control of the JNA, the 80th Motorised Brigade, where they were guarded.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: General, before the crime was committed, were these people in the hands of the army?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When they were killed, were they in the hands of the army?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In the examination-in-chief, did you speak about your meeting with Mrksic who, according to what you said, had said, "Had we known what would have happened, we never would have handed them over to those local organs over there"? Is that right or is that not right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In connection with Ovcara, you talked to the then military prosecutor who was conducting a detailed investigation. Did he tell you that the trial had not started yet because the Prosecution had established --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... make a complaint in the way the matter is put, but that evidence was not given in chief and it was not given in chief quite specifically. I confined my -- as far as I can recall, I confined my evidence of what Mrksic said to the fact that he said at the end of the discussion, We found out what they did to them, we swore to keep it secret. Actually, on reflection, he may have given the longer bit first, but that was the passage I relied upon and the only passage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We ought to have the record right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I now actually can't immediately recall whether, although that was my intention to get that passage out as something upon which I relied, the witness may have given voluntarily a longer answer, which of course --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What my note is, is in 1998, Mrksic told the witness in answer to what happened at Ovcara, "I swear by my children, had I known what they would do to them, we would never have handed them over."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In which case my recollection is wrong. My intention remains as stated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And then he was asked, to complete the note, why he didn't inform the line of communication. Mrksic said when he found out what they'd done, they swore to remain silent.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Grateful.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very good that you reminded everybody of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Since those who knew about it kept silent about it, isn't that right, how could anybody else have known about it?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know which period you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Until it was found out. Considerably later, considerably after these events actually took place.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said when I first found out about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. You talked to the then military prosecutor who was carrying out a detailed investigation. Did he tell you then that the trial had not started because the prosecution had established that Radic, Mrksic, and Sljivancanin were not responsible for the crimes in Ovcara? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And that it was established who the suspects are and that the materials were handed over to the civilian prosecutor's office in charge.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. We are not now going into any explanations as to whether one crime can justify another crime. There should be no discussion about that. But I would like you to answer me the following question: Like then, what happened before and what happened after, is it correct that Marin Vidic, nicknamed Bili, who was a commissioner of the Croatian government for Vukovar whose diary you seized when you arrested him, he was held accountable after that, but you did have a diary that you seized, and he was a high official of the HDZ and of the authorities in the Srem and Baranja region, and you saw from that that he levelled grave accusations against Mercep, that he was the main guilty party for all the conflicts in that area. Is that right or that is not right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what he said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you have any information about the following: That as far back as 1990, the meeting at the Trpinje road, where Seks and the others were, a plan was made to have Serbs laid off and intimidated and thrown out of the area altogether, and if all of this proved to be unsuccessful, that they should ultimately be liquidated? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about a plan having been established, but I know that this had been advocated. And within that concept, groups for silent Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. liquidations were established.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: To the best of your knowledge, General, these groups for silent liquidations, how many Serbs did they kill before there was any kind of rebellion in that area, any kind of rebellion of the Serb population against this violence and terror?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have this information about the killed civilians. I know and you also presented some figures concerning the killings of officers and soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But you do have to have some knowledge about civilians as a citizen, if not as a security officer. You don't have any knowledge about that?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't, unfortunately. I'm not saying that no such thing happened, but I don't have any information about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But you know that this did happen and that there was a considerable number of such cases?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, all right. Isn't it true that this same Marin Vidic, in this same diary that you confiscated when you arrested him for Borovo Selo, Serbs are not the ones to be blamed, he says, and the Croat authorities did not take any action to stop Mercep although everything was known about the bad things he did.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is in his statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know about attacks against the garrison in Vinkovci when over 6.000 projectiles landed on the garrison, according to the report that was established then?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know about that. This figure is correct, and that is in the context of -- in the context of what happened then when a wax figure was made to the likeness of the head of the commander of that garrison.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you something about Dubrovnik. In Western Herzegovina, were armed -- were armed units of the HOS established?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. That is the first half of 1991. And on the 24th of May, they were discovered or, rather, three truckloads of weapons that were brought from the warehouse in Lucka to Capljina, and they were distributed to members of the HOS.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that from -- that from Dubrovnik people from Metkovic and Opuzen came, members of the National Guards Corps?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. And then the president of the Municipal Assembly of Neum, the Minister of the Interior of Bosnia-Herzegovina asked for a meeting in order to intervene to have this prevented, that is to say so that Bosnia would not be dragged into the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that members of the ZNG in Dubrovnik made a garrison although Dubrovnik was a demilitarised city? There were no military facilities, no military installations, no military crews in the municipality of Dubrovnik or the coast area or Konavle until they militarised it? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had information that there were armed forces of the ZNG in Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that precisely after these complaints that you just mentioned of the president of Neum, which is the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina - this is the only place where Bosnia-Herzegovina has an exit to the sea - that on the 29th of November, 1991, from the airport in Mostar, a military pilot was kidnapped, Dragan Stojicevic, whereas a policeman of the MUP of Bosnia-Herzegovina was killed, who was securing a bridge in Capljina?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That happened on the 28th of November. And the captain was Dragan Stojcinovic. That piece of information is correct. And he was later detained in the military prison in Split. It is also true that this policeman of Bosnia-Herzegovina who was securing the bridge in Capljina was killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Considering what you just said about the beginning of the year 1991 and the creation of armed formations, was it clear to you as security organs that there was an intent to annex Herzegovina to Croatia?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that there was an official declaration or a written stance to that effect, but the entire climate and the events that happened in this area reflected the situation as if Herzegovina was already a part of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All these operations conducted by Bobetko, is it true that there were no defence of Dubrovnik? Is it true that they amounted to a division of Bosnia and Herzegovina in an effort to inflame a war in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say that, because this came at a later time in relation to my service.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know anything at all about the reasons why the JNA blocked Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the military point of view, I know that on the 20th of September, 1991, since the garrisons in the military naval district were blocked and the military port of Lora in Split, parts of the Uzice Corps were brought there and parts of the Podgorica Corps were introduced into Bosnia and Herzegovina. And a reinforced security detail of the airport in Mostar was taken over. And from Nevesinje towards Mostar, and from Gacko towards Capljina. Forces of the JNA emerged onto the left bank of the Neretva. That was supposed to reflect a threat and a sign of their alertness and readiness, for the forces of the military naval district to be deblocked from the rear, whereas the forces of the ZNG which entered Dubrovnik were practically in the rear of these forces which had emerged onto the bank of the Neretva River. And they started actions with these forces, because attacks were mounted in Eastern Herzegovina. When forces were brought in from Stolac towards Capljina, an attack was mounted on the column of the 3rd Partisan Division and several members of the JNA were killed on that occasion. Also, in another village further to the west, there was another attack on a military unit, resulting in about ten or 11 deaths. So attacks had already started in the rear and on the flank of the forces that had emerged on the Neretva River. That's as much as I know about the military aspect.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So what you know, does it confirm that the JNA mounted no attack? On the contrary, it was the target of an attack?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These cases that I spoke about are what I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So an attack was mounted on JNA units.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said exactly which places and which case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let's try and clarify the witness's evidence. As I understand it, you're saying that -- General, that the JNA was being reinforced in order to reflect a threat, and then you say there were actions in Eastern Herzegovina. Can you tell us from your information, rather than what you might have read about or anything of that sort after the event, but from your information at the time, can you tell us what was happening around Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Specifically as far as actions around Dubrovnik are concerned, I had no direct observations reported to me by security organs. I received my information through the line of communication in security organs about security aspects. And in cases of attacks on JNA units, I got information if sabotage units were involved. And I mentioned this attack on the column of the 3rd Partisan Division which was going via Stolac towards Capljina. As far as actions specifically around Dubrovnik are concerned, I have no knowledge of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Do you have an explanation as to why it was blocked in the first place? As far as I understood your explanation, although you have no knowledge of direct action, your explanation why Dubrovnik was blocked was that it was an intent to exert pressure to deblock barracks that had been blocked at the time and the garrisons that were jeopardised.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Explain then why.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said -- I said that the forces were located, deployed on the flank and in the rear of the JNA units. So Dubrovnik was not blocked in order to deblock the Lora port. It was not a parallel activity.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In fact, forces of the ZNG were on the side and behind the forces that emerged on the Neretva River. And part of these forces, not from Dubrovnik but from those inserted from Metkovic, mounted an attack on certain columns of the JNA that had been extended, stretched in the process of insertion. I suppose that because actions had already started from Dubrovnik against the JNA forces, this is the way the military operations developed in this area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You just said that there were actions mounted from Dubrovnik against the JNA and that is why the conflict in Dubrovnik started.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that tyres were set on fire in order to attract media attention and to insinuate the JNA setting Dubrovnik on fire by artillery?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is that true?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to our information, it was true. A lot of smoke was raised and a media show was created in order to create mistrust and to get the international public opinion to condemn the actions against Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You explained -- let me not interpret you because we have everything on tape and transcripts; you just explained the real reasons for these operations. Tell me, give me a straightforward answer to a short question: Did Serbia have anything to do with actions around Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Let us move to another topic. This is not the best map I've seen. It is a map of demarcation of military districts in the SFRY, but since claims were made here that Serbia intended to become a Greater Serbia and to set some sort of new borders with Karlovac, Karlobag, Virovitica being mentioned all over the place, have you ever heard anyone mentioning any points, lines, and so on and so forth to which Serbia should extend in Croatia or which JNA should conquer in Croatia in order for Serbia to become larger? Have you heard anything about the idea of Greater Serbia?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't hear it from anyone in the military leadership. But as an ordinary citizen, I heard many stories about it at rallies, and I quoted examples in my previous testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What rallies?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I already said at what rallies. The rallies where it was said where there are Serbian graves, there are Serbian lands.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You mean Vuk Draskovic and others. Did you hear anyone from the government or the Socialist Party saying that?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'll skip some questions. Is it true, General, that in Bosnia and Herzegovina, as far as back as in mid-September 1990, the JNA discovered paramilitary organisations of the Party of Democratic Action headed by Izetbegovic?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mid-September 1990.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 17th of September, to be precise.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that on the 15th October 1990 and the 24th December 1990, two sessions of the military leadership and the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina were held to discuss the security situation and the prevention of internecine conflict?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And this paramilitary organisation of the SDA was based on Islamic fundamentalism; is that correct? In September 1990.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot speak as to what it was based on. I can quote elements from their organisational orders. Basically, it was all about the defence of Muslims and the areas they populated.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In September 1990, tell me, who was it who jeopardised Muslims and the areas they populated? Was it, in other words, defence or something else?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not September 1990. September 1991. So that was discovered in September 1991. And from that order on organisation, it transpires characteristically that the Patriotic League of Nations had 11 subregional and one main military staff, and two staffs, one for Sandzak and one for Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So two on the territory of Serbia and nine on the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina which were populated by Muslims?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not only areas populated by Muslims, but according to the then territorial division of Bosnia-Herzegovina, these subregional staffs were formed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So on the entire territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And in two areas of Serbia, Sandzak and Kosovo; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what did that tell you?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That Muslims too were organising themselves for defence outside the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: To defend themselves from whom?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As it said there, from the aggressor JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you, the JNA, attack Muslims anywhere?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not as long as I was in the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You were in the army until the spring 1992, as far as I understand.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you attack Muslims anywhere?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did anyone attack Muslims, for instance, in the territory of Serbia since they had in Sandzak a centre for defence? Not in 1991, 1992, but even later, 1999, and 2000, did anyone attack them anywhere ever?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You know about the case at the railway station.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You mean Strpce?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Strpce is in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, as you well know.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That's where the railroad passes. And you know and I informed Stoltenberg that after this event, although it is the territory of another republic, I ordered a platoon to be stationed there to guard this station so that another scoundrel could not stop a train again and kill our citizens.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not commenting on this from the territorial angle. I'm just saying that Muslims from the territory of Serbia were killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, not Serbia. Do you know that at that time we charged that it was done intentionally, to cause a conflict between Muslims and Serbs in Serbia and transfer the conflict across the border?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was in the military prison at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Then I will not question you about it.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But I know that this investigation was not conducted in the best possible way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, since I asked you about these two sessions of the military leadership and the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina about the security situation, is it true that Izetbegovic, in order to accuse the JNA as being a Serbian army and no longer a Yugoslav army, ordered in 1991 that military records should be put away, that conscripts from Bosnia-Herzegovina should not be allowed to join the JNA, and that in cahoots with Tudjman, he addressed a general call to officers not to go to the JNA or, rather, to desert it? Are you aware of what?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Military records in those days were kept in all the republics in the Secretariats for National Defence. That's right. And the order was from the General Staff to take over those records, and that order was not observed, not complied with, because the records were put away. And it is Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. true that Tudjman made a call in favour of obstructing the mobilisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And when was this? Was it in middle of 1991 when both among the Muslims and from the top Croatian leadership there was insistence on obstructing the JNA?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Particularly as from the 15th of September, 1991, and onwards. So from the beginning of war operations against military facilities in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Since we have established that I could not have influence over the military leadership like General Kadijevic, for instance.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think you could have.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And General Kadijevic was in his position until January 1992.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Until the 8th of January, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So was there any possibility for anyone from Serbia and I personally to influence the changes that had taken place up until then? Any kind of personnel changes in the army.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Until the end of 1991, there was no possibility. There were attempts, but not -- not really.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And who made those attempts?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said Zoran Sokolovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did he give a name of somebody that you need to appoint or replace or did he just inquire generally about things?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He inquired into general information about generals.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: He didn't attempt to impose anyone on you or to remove anyone.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I broke off the conversation straight away.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know which conversation you stopped.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I'm just saying I don't know how the conversation would have developed if I had allowed it to develop.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And when Kadijevic explained that he was getting on and that his health was not at its best, do you remember the explanation that he gave for leaving the position of Federal Secretary and that he was succeeded by Blagoje Hadzic?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Blagoje Adzic, had he been anyway the number two man in the military leadership?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did anyone influence the appointment of Adzic?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was some influence over him when he retired.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And when did Adzic retire?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the 8th of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Can we then state that on the basis of what you are testifying about, until the 8th of May when Blagoje Adzic retired, there was no theoretical possibility for someone from Serbia and I personally to influence the army, the JNA? Is that right or not?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not right. I've already said, I don't know whether it was in private session or public session, but never mind, I can say this in public session as well, I mentioned the example of the retirement of 33 generals in February 1992 when General Blagoje Adzic addressed you in connection with the reasons for the retirement of my deputy. So he didn't address himself to Branko Kostic who signed the decrees but he addressed you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You've already explained that. But would you allow for the possibility for Blagoje Adzic to address me for me to intervene with the Presidency? Because I'm not the decision-maker. Someone may address someone to ask him for his assistance, in fact, for a particular case that he needs assistance for. Would you allow for that possibility or do you believe that I was the one deciding that you should be pensioned off or someone else?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Blagoje Adzic had authority as a senior officer and as a personality. And of course in view of that position, he could have easily addressed Branko Kostic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How do you know that he didn't?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because I was present when he called you up and you told him to come.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But how do you know that he didn't call up Branko Kostic, and Boro Jovic, and Bogic Bogicevic and all the other members of the Presidency over there and me as well as president of Serbia? How do you know who else he called on? Why do you believe that it was only me?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because he spoke only to you and he didn't mention having talked to anyone else about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, he did speak to me. Are you claiming he spoke to no one else?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot claim that but I do claim that he didn't tell me that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you're claiming that he didn't tell you that he had spoken to anyone else?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He's an honourable man, and I have no doubts that he would give any false information here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But let's continue. In connection with the events in Bosnia and Herzegovina, is it true that it was agreed at the Presidency session that a joint plan be devised to disarm all paramilitary units in Bosnia-Herzegovina? And this was on the 19th of January, 1991.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. On the 24th of December, 1991, at a session of the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the military leadership, it was agreed that such a plan be prepared. The plan was reviewed on the 19th of January, 1992, together with the MUP of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what happened?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our joint proposal was - that is of the security administration and the MUP of Bosnia and Herzegovina - that the plan could succeed only if adequate political support is given to it by all three national leaders in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and that support was not forthcoming.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: They couldn't agree?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Each one of them claimed that the plan was good but that his people did not have weapons but that the other two people's did. And because that plan was not accepted, I went, on the 5th of February, to talk to Mr. Alija Izetbegovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me before that, please, since you mentioned the Patriotic League of Nations and its headquarters and arming, this Patriotic League of Nations was a Muslim terrorist organisation, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You've already asked me that, and I said I cannot give you an overall answer for the whole organisation, but in that organisation and each subregional headquarters, there was a special sabotage unit. So special diversionist terrorist units were formed in each of these headquarters of this so-called Patriotic League of people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Subregional. I see, subregional terrorist platoons.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Diversionist terrorist platoons.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. And this league of people or nation implies only Muslims, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. In the programme, they allowed for the possibility for any member of the people of Bosnia-Herzegovina to take part, and there were individual cases, small -- in small numbers of people who joined the Patriotic League who were not Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you mentioned terrorist units or, rather, sabotage terrorist units. So not to split hairs as to the difference between the two, is it true that Izetbegovic at first denied the existence of these headquarters, but when you showed him the evidence, he said that he would conduct a detailed investigation and the perpetrators would be punished and he did nothing about it? I've asked you several questions now. Is it true that Izetbegovic denied it, and when you showed him the evidence, that he said he would look into it and the perpetrators would be punished? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is right that at first he denied it, and when a part of the evidence was shown to him, he said that he had not been aware of it and that he would take measures. And he added that for as long as he was president and for as long as he was consulted, nobody would attack the JNA. According to our information, in the next month, some measures were carried out upon his orders. Cases were looked into of the abuse of funds that had been collected for weapons, and they were probably investigating our presence and how we had managed to discover this organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did he keep his promise that no one would attack the JNA?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The JNA was attacked for the first time in an organised manner at the JNA centre in Sarajevo when Izetbegovic was not present in Sarajevo. He was on his way back from Lisbon, on the plane. And that is when an all-out conflict started between the JNA and the Patriotic League in Sarajevo. The next day we had the event in Dobrovoljacka Street.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So that is when attacks and killing of members of the JNA started.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a case of a -- when eight soldiers were captured from the Sarajevo garrison, and we established later that they were executed in the city's park by members of the Green Berets, so special forces. These were individual attacks, but the all-out generalised attack started with the JNA centre and onwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So there were individual cases following Izetbegovic's promise, and this all-out attack occurred while he was on the plane, flying back from Lisbon. Do you know how long he was in Lisbon?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know when he left. I know when he was on his way back.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, surely you can assume that this was a brief visit to Lisbon, and the fact that he was on the plane at the time of attack does not mean that he has no responsibility for this. The Patriotic League was under his command, was it not?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the political sense, in the operative, direct responsibility was Ejub Ganic, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was he his deputy?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was his deputy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did he transfer to him the position of Supreme Commander on television in fact?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in the barracks in Lukavica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So Izetbegovic is directly responsible for the crimes committed by this so-called Patriotic League of Nations when absolutely no one was jeopardised -- jeopardising anyone in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The witness can't give evidence of this sort. This may be a matter for the Trial Chamber, but it sounds like a judgement or conclusion which the accused is trying to have made, and it's not a matter for the witness to make.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. May. I will just focus on facts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So please, General, let's economise with time. Is it true that on the 6th of April, 1991, a rally for Yugoslavia was organised in front of the Holiday Inn hotel? On the 6th of April, 1991, a rally of support for Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I'm not sure whether it was on the 5th or the 6th.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Let's say the 5th or the 6th. Is it true that at this rally attended by about 100.000 people, which is an enormous number for Sarajevo, you will admit, among whom there were miners from Ilijas, Kakanj, Breza who had come to support Yugoslavia? Is it true that propaganda was used to say that Chetniks would open fire from the premises of the Serbia Democratic Party at the participants from behind?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was a planned provocation through certain members of the Green Berets who were accommodated in the building of the secondary technical school next to the Holiday Inn, and they fired a shot into the crowd from behind, and the allegation was made that it was the Chetniks, members of the SDS that were firing from the Holiday Inn, because the premises of the SDS used to be there before, which had already been evacuated.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: They had already left it then?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were some people there still.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And tell me, the people that opened fire, as you established, and you said that they were the Green Berets, to make it known here, to make it clear, who are those Green Berets?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Green Berets were the first name given to this institution which later became the Patriotic League. Typical of them were the green berets that they wore on certain occasions, and they also wore green scarves as a mark of identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: This unit was operating from the municipality Stari Grad. Was that a terrorist act? Not just a provocation but a terrorist act?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've given you the facts. I cannot make any judgements.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was that the first case of fire being opened by the Muslims to blame the Serbs, and then came the bread line, Vasa Miskin, Merkale 1, Merkale 2? Was this the beginning of a practice to kill one's own people and put the blame on the Serbs? Was this the first case?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about the subsequent events, Merkale and everything else that happened I know only from the media, but regarding this rally, one man was not killed but wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The fact that he was wounded was not the -- the merit for that does not belong to the person who opened fire?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That's a very serious allegation, as you appreciate, to suggest that one side was firing on, killing its own members as a provocation. Will you tell us what the basis your knowledge of that incident is? I take it you weren't there in Sarajevo at the time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I wasn't in Sarajevo, but I had security organs in Sarajevo who intercepted a message through radio communications used by the Green Berets, indicating that the operation should begin. And then came the shot. And we also found a TV clipping. I think this was Caco - that was his nickname - and a shot was taken of the secondary school building from which they came out. So there was an audio recording from radio communications and a part of a TV clipping, showing them coming out of the secondary school. Then there was also a part of a special MUP unit that immediately stormed the Holiday Inn, and I know of the order that everything should be broken up inside, that nothing should be left intact. I think three or four persons were arrested who were in the SDS premises. And forensic evidence was never produced to prove that they had opened fire; paraffin gloves, bullet casings or anything like that. And afterwards they were released. One of those persons is now living in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So these were some not very important members of the SDS who happened to be in the premises. They were arrested. They were blamed for the shooting, and then, without any explanation, they were released; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Because they had no grounds to press charges. And you know full well this was committed by the Green Berets. Is there any doubt in your mind about it?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, none. I have some names also who led the operation, who was in charge of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did Juka Prazina enter the technical school building?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He was the one who ordered fire to be opened from the school building.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell us briefly, who was Juka Prazina?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One of the criminals, local criminals who was released from prison and who joined the Green Berets, similar to such cases in other areas, Croatia and elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but I'm asking you about Juka Prazina now and that he was a member of the Green Berets. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And did people from Sandzak headed by Mirza Jamakovic, a member of the SUP of Bosnia-Herzegovina, break into the Holiday Inn?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And their task was to destroy the Holiday Inn and the SDS Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. premises?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And they arrested those three men? They found -- releasing them without any explanation later on; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now for a moment let me mention the event in Dobrovoljacka Street because of Izetbegovic's strategy that we have mentioned. Was there quite reliable information from the military security service that the operation in Dobrovoljacka Street were also carried out by the Green Berets and in the operative sense is it true that the direct commander of the operation was Zaim Backovic, known as Zagi, who was, at the time, deputy commander of the Territorial Defence, a deputy of Hasan Efendic who was Staff Commander at the time?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I have asked you several questions in one. But the gist of it is the event in Dobrovoljacka Street, who committed that act and what happened?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was committed by the Green Berets of the Stari Grad municipality that were under the command in the operative sense of Emin Svrakic, and Zaim Backovic was at the command post, if I can call it that, in the Presidency building on the 2nd floor, in an office there, and Alija Izetbegovic's son was also there, Bakir. His name is Bakir. And Ejub Ganic would come there too to monitor the situation regarding the pull-out of the command of the 2nd Military District through Dobrovoljacka Street.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So, General --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm going to stop you. It's past time for a break. We'll adjourn -- we will adjourn now for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: General, is it being challenged that that crime in Dobrovoljacka Street was commanded directly from Izetbegovic's office, from the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina, to the best of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was not Izetbegovic's office. This was a small office across the corridor from the meeting room.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When I say "office," I don't mean his actual office where he sits, the room where he sits, i mean the president of the Presidency whose president he was. So I'm talking about his seat, his headquarters, his office in that sense.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, before we move on, I'm not seeking to stop this line of questioning, but the Chamber will observe that the witness did not deal with Bosnia in his examination-in-chief for reasons that he explained to us when he was being prepared to give evidence. Questions that are asked on Bosnia now will no doubt be reflected in the scope and possibly even the timing of re-examination because it's basically covering a whole new topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We're not going to stop the examination, it may be relevant to issues which we have yet to cover, and the accused should have the opportunity of calling the evidence on it and asking questions. Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, in relation to what Mr. Nice said just now, I believe it is highly relevant to establish how the conflicts started in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We're not going to stop you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that the unit of the Green Berets on the ground was commanded by Mustafa Hajrulahovic, nicknamed Talijan, and the unit of the Patriotic League that we already mentioned and defined, Stari Grad, was commanded by Emin Svrakic, and according to the vertical line on the ground, he was actually subordinated to Hasan Cengic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about the vertical line, that it was subordinated to Hasan Cengic. These two persons you mentioned are persons about whom we did have this information. And as far as Hasan Cengic is concerned, I know they came to the building of the Presidency after the command function was transferred to Ejub Ganic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
