utterances.text: When you talk about the transfer of this command function, is it correct that on the 2nd of February, in the evening, when the JNA centre was attacked, when Fikret Abdic came from Zenica to Sarajevo and spoke to the people on radio and television, addressing an appeal for peace - that was around 1955 hours - after that, Alija Izetbegovic was seen and heard from the Lukavica barracks, and he transferred all presidential powers to Ejub Ganic, and practically Ejub Ganic assumed the position of presidency?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was probably a slip of the tongue. It was not the 2nd of February, it was the 2nd of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Oh, of course, that's right, it was the 2nd of May.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What you said is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And the attack against the military column in Dobrovoljacka Street, was this attack commanded by Ejub Ganic himself and did he afterwards state in public that he was actually in command?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that he came to this command room from which the communications went to the units on the ground, and I know that he gave statements later that allegedly it was not agreed that the entire command of the 2nd Army should get out, led by General Kukanjac, rather, only General Kukanjac was supposed to be exchanged for Alija Izetbegovic and that there was no agreement reached that the army should leave barracks, that they were supposed to remain there under blockade. And this is how he was trying to justify the attack against that column.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: This column of soldiers leaving the barracks, they were not engaged in any kind of combat operation. They were simply withdrawing from that barracks that was under blockade.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No one fired a single gunshot from that column.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that officers and soldiers were dragged out of vehicles, that four officers and one woman and one young soldier were killed immediately while the others were transferred to the physical education centre where they were interrogated by the commander of the military police, Kerim Loncarevic and Fikret Muslimanovic, a former JNA colonel?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Fikret Muslimovic, not Muslimanovic. That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that with regard to the liquidations of eight JNA soldiers in the city park, according to reliable knowledge, the arrest of these soldiers and their later execution was carried out by a person under the pseudonym of Miso who was a member of the military police of this so-called Patriotic People's League with the immediate assistance of Ismet Bajramovic, nicknamed Celo, who was a criminal and released from prison before that in order to join the Green Berets?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I already referred to this incident earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So it is correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is operative knowledge as to who are the persons who carried out the liquidation. It is correct that eight soldiers were liquidated.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that Izetbegovic, on the 26th of April, 1992, in Skopje at a meeting with Branko Kostic, inter alia all sorts of aspects were discussed there, he said in Bosnia-Herzegovina there were no paramilitary units and that when he was shown the order of Hasan Efendic as the new commander of the Bosnian TO which ordered the blockade of all military facilities in Bosnia-Herzegovina and attacks against units that would try to leave the mentioned facilities, he answered that this was done without his knowledge and approval?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not at that meeting, and I do not know how it went. I know that Blagoje Adzic, General Blagoje Adzic gave us information when he came back from that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was that the information he gave you?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that you talked to Izetbegovic on the 5th of February, 1992, in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that after an unsuccessful agreement with the MUP of Bosnia-Herzegovina to have the paramilitary units of Bosnia-Herzegovina disarmed, the Chief of General Staff decided that you should talk to Izetbegovic and tell him about the facts that the military service knew about the preparation of this so-called Patriotic People's League that had to do with attacks against the JNA?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The reasons why I went to this meeting are partially correct. One was that the plan dated the 19th of January was not accepted, and the second one was that after that we sent information regard -- information to the then four members of the Presidency of Yugoslavia, and we proposed to take an independent action of disarmament. However, the Presidency returned this information to us without any position of their own taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me about the preparations of the so-called Patriotic People's League regarding attacks against the JNA. Is it true that during this conversation, Izetbegovic for a long time refused to admit that this kind of organisation existed in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina at all, and only when part of the original documents were shown to him, he said that these paramilitary units, objectively speaking, could not be disarmed any longer?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean his conversation with me?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that he said then that it should be made sure that they do not attack and block the JNA but then actually in the second half of April, it is precisely the commander of the Territorial Defence that wrote a directive about the general blockade of the JNA in Bosnia-Herzegovina? Is that right or is that not right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The general blockade of military facilities in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: General, do you have any knowledge regarding the armament of the HDZ in Slavonski Brod and the SDS in the area of Derventa in 1991 and in 1992 while you still held your post?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did have information about this entire area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know who Mujkic Resad and Sefik are?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know of the name of Sefik, and I think the last name is Mujkic. I don't know the name Resad.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know anything about two trucks with Ljubljana licence plates that in March 1992 arrived in Slavonski Brod and were then transferred to Derventa, accompanied or escorted by the Bosnian MUP?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not have this information. I can't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know who Petar Ocausanin is?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ocausanin was a security organ, I think, at the Brcko garrison, if I'm not mistaken.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: He was a security organ at the JNA barracks in Derventa, precisely when these trucks came, when this transport took place.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Possibly he was in Derventa. I know that he was in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that Resid Mujkic at that time was president of the SDA for Slavonski Brod and vice-president for all of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know that the owner of the privately owned company called Colt was precisely this Resid Mujkic from Derventa and that this company bought 1.798.390 ammunitions?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was not information. This was launched through a campaign that had to do with the alleged arming of Croats via the Muslims in that area. I don't know about that. I don't have any operative information in this regard.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Do you know then about your own report of the 5th of August 1991 that you submitted to the General Staff regarding the situation -- I have it here. It says, handwritten, "Head of the security administration, General Aco Vasiljevic submits this report to the General Staff." And then there is further typewritten text. At the General Staff, on the 5th of August, 1991. Do you remember this presentation of yours and the situation you described?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that. I remember that on the 6th of August. I have that written down, actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Possibly you have a mistake because you have the 5th of August here. Perhaps the meeting was held then.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what the topic was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm going to read this to you, and then I'm going to give it to you to have a look at it. You say that: "In Croatia, the JNA was proclaimed an occupational force and that it should be expected in the coming period major efforts would be made to name the JNA as an aggressor. The leadership of Croatia is in a great hurry in order to provoke a war with the JNA so that Croatia would be portrayed as a victim of aggression, and in this way, they would cause a military intervention of the West in order to protect "democracy." This is probably one of the main reasons why in the critical areas, according to the orders of the MUP and the ZNG, the JNA is attacked on the sly."

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember having submitted such a report. Perhaps these are notes that I made regarding a presentation that was made by some other JNA officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. So a presentation made by some other officer. I'll give you these -- this outline so that you can see it because it says here that this is an outline of what you said at this meeting. Now, are these facts and assessments correct, the ones that were presented?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They are not in dispute.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What was that? They are not in dispute?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They are not in dispute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let's see the document so we can have the matter clarified.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are going to have it clarified. I just want to read something else out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Here it says, "In BiH, the legitimate and legal authorities extended for another seven days the sending of conscripts to the JNA. The party organisation of paramilitary units of the HDZ, SDA are under way and party officials are attacking the JNA in an increasingly impudent manner. The units, especially in Bosnia-Herzegovina, are constantly being observed by the Croatian intelligence services. The main organiser of the anti-army activities in Bosnia-Herzegovina is Jerko Doko, the Minister of Defence of Bosnia-Herzegovina. The agreement between the SDS and the MBO does have prospects if Alija Izetbegovic accepts this reality in order to alleviate the situation."

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that part.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And then you say in -- you talk about Serbia, about the activity of some opposition parties, that the Serbs do not have an interest in being under the symbol of the communist JNA. And you quote the Serbian Renewal Movement there, the SPO, and you say that the objective of all of that is to compromise and break up the JNA, and at the same time the creation of the Serbian Guard is the creation of a paramilitary formation that will forcibly take over power in Serbia and do away with the JNA. As for what the SPO wants to do with active military personnel of the JNA is something that is spoken about in public. And then you quote: "We are going to keep in the Serbian Guard persons up to the rank of captain, physicians, and the like, and the rest we are going to deal with in our very own way." Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not the last part.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Have a look at this. This is an outline of your very own presentation. Perhaps this is going to jog your memory. What I quoted to you just now, it's at the end of page 3, where you speak about the attacks of the MUP on the sly. They attack the JNA. It's what I quoted to you about the attacks against the JNA. So you can have a look at the entire Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: General, would you look at that, just remind yourself of it --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: -- and then there will be a few questions from the Trial Chamber about it. Could you tell us, first of all, General, what is it that you're looking at.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I don't remember this document in this form, not at all. I don't even see my handwriting here. This was done as some sort of outline for a presentation, a speech. I usually wrote down all my speeches in my own notebook and only very rarely did I have written text to read out, a typewritten text. But a part from what the accused read out here is correct. However, the outlines, as I see them here, I used to write down in my own notebook, and I usually asked somebody -- it was not my custom to ask somebody else to type out my presentations. Whatever I had to read out at meetings, I usually wrote down in my notebook. I don't remember that it was on the 5th of August. I remember the 6th of August. That is the first date I remember. And I remember it by the fact that it was the first time we got information about illegal weapons in the Constanza port, and that is when I had a meeting in General Kadijevic's office. I can read the whole text now and see if anything corresponds to my recollection or does not correspond, but I don't remember this text as such.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment. Just a moment. Is there anything in the document to connect it with you, to show that it is your text?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I haven't read it in its entirety, and I can categorically state that I did not draw it up. This text can be something prepared by a team to be given to me before I make my report. I repeat, this text or any similar text is something that I never had before a meeting as something I was supposed to read out. I usually made my own preparations for meetings. I noted down whatever I had to say in my own notebook. And when I made my reports, I didn't read from a page. I spoke --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I extemporised. If you allow me just one more word. It is customary, according to the procedure in the security administration, that if something like this was typewritten for the head of administration, it should be written military secret, strictly confidential, copy such-and-such number. So in the right top corner it would be written routinely. There would not necessarily be a stamp if it were a working draft, but there would be this mark of secrecy. Another unusual thing is that at the end of the text, in the lower left-hand side, there are no initials of the person who drafted the text and no initials of the person who typed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, may the witness, possibly at the next break, have the opportunity to review it in full? It's always asking a lot of a witness to look at what I think it is a five-page document when he's in the witness box. If he can review it at the next break, possibly extending the next break by a couple of minutes, I would be very grateful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Of course. What we'll do is this: We'll have this marked for identification. But before we do, there was another document which was produced by the accused which was the, I think, the ethnic structures of the JNA generals. That will be given the next exhibit number, and this document which the witness has can have the following one. Perhaps the registrar will just deal with that formally.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The list would be marked Defence Exhibit 101, and this letter will be marked Defence Exhibit 102 marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: General, would you during the next break review that document when you have a chance to do so rather more at your leisure. Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Let us put aside the usual format of this document, because it says, "Outlines for the report of the head of the security administration." That was you. Let us put this aside. We will not debate now whether it is your document or not, considering at that Mr. May gave you instructions to read it during the break. Please bear in mind that I will be asking you questions regarding the content of these outlines, whether various things are correct or not in view of the time of this report. You said that what I quoted was correct, but please read out the entire document, and you will tell me whether certain things are correct or not.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that some of the things were correct. I recognised them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Okay. You recognised some of them. But I will ask you during the break to point out what is not accurate, because the material truth is what matters, not the format of the document which you may have forgotten, as well as whether somebody else drafted this outline for you. That's not what matters. What matters is the content. At that time, is it true -- saw unprovoked attacks on the JNA, the JNA centre, the Dobrovoljacka Street, is it true that at that time Croatian units made incursion into Bosnia and Herzegovina and carried out the liquidation of Serbs a while later but this was the first major attack in the village of Sijekovac, Bosanski Brod on the 27th of March 1992?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was that the first attack by armed formations of Croatia in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and in general, the first attack of any armed forces outside the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before that, there was the destruction of the bridge of Orasje on the Sava River which linked Bosnia and Herzegovina with Croatia, and I think there was some firings from the territory of Croatia towards the Bosnian side. However, this major incursion was one of the first.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that this action was carried by the 108th Brigade of the National Guard Corps of Croatia which operated on the territory of Slavonski Brod and that the commander of that so-called Patriotic People's League for Northern Bosnia, Vahid Karavelic, later general, in Bosnia and Herzegovina had in his possession original documentation on the purchase of weapons and ammunition for the Patriotic People's League for the area of Zvornik, precisely from the warehouses, from the depots of that 108th Brigade of the ZNG?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, one question at a time. Now, what do you want the witness to answer in relation to this?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: First, is it true that, according to your knowledge, this operation was carried out by the 108th Brigade of the ZNG?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And is it true that the purchase of weapons and ammunition for the units of that so-called Patriotic People's League was also made from the depot of that brigade, from the area of Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the documentation found with the then Captain Vahid Karavelic, it is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And tell me, is it true that the incursion into Bosanski Brod was then carried out with 30 vehicles, 15 tanks? And then in the village of Sijekovac, Serbian families of Zecevic, Basic, Radovanovic were liquidated?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: First of all, 30 vehicles, 15 tanks. Do you know if that's right or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't tell you now the exact figure, how many tanks or how many vehicles were used, nor can I know these families by name, the families that were liquidated. But I know that it was a combat group of some force which had military combat vehicles, and I know about the crime committed against local Serbs - bodies were later thrown into the Sava River - but I don't have the details quoted by the accused.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Okay. We can move on now. Considering that the Croatian leadership and Izetbegovic both wanted war on Kosovo, is it true that the security service of the army much earlier discovered first illegal groups in Kosovo within the JNA?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. The first group, the first such group in the JNA was discovered in the beginning of 1991 -- 1981.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Back in 1981?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before the demonstrations in Kosovo on the 11th of March, the first such group was exposed in the JNA with about 20 members, and it had its basis in the garrison of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that your service in 1994 exposed the military organisation of Albanian emigres around the world with national centres?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In July 1984, a unification of all illegal organisations in Kosovo was discovered. That was carried out on the 17th of February, 1982. And the name of this new unified organisation was the Movement for the Albanian Socialist Republic of Yugoslavia or, in an abbreviation, MASRY.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that your service in 1990 exposed illegal importation of arms into Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I talked about the import of pistols through the Kintex company for Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it true, General, that in 1990 and 1991, neither generals nor officers of the JNA were involved in politics but engaged in their professional duties, expecting the Presidency of the SFRY and political factors to find political solutions?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For all I know, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You know the name of Candic who was a security organ in your service?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I want to ask you not in relation to his statement, because that's not your job, but in relation to only one part of his statement where he quoted you, presumably. He said here that at a meeting of security organs, you spoke angrily about the fact that Milosevic is conducting activities geared at getting generals to sign an oath of loyalty to him. Is it true that you said that Milosevic was asking generals of the JNA to sign an oath of loyalty to him?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That's not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Then I can skip a number of questions. When you speak about the officers who were in the army of Republika Srpska or the army of the Republic of Serbian Krajina or in general about the events which you can competently speak about, is it true that it is precisely your security administration availed itself of the opportunity whenever a former member of the JNA went to visit his family from the Republic of Serbian Krajina or Republika Srpska, to invite him for an informal meeting to find out about the situation, gather information, and so on and so forth? Since they had no formal competencies over such officers, they used various informal occasions to contact with them and gather information from such conversations or interviews; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not in the army of Yugoslavia then, but from what I know, they were not even invited to visit their former superiors for such interviews. I know, however, that they came of their own accord, possibly because they wanted to find out whether a place would be available for them again in the Yugoslav army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that General Mladic, as a high-ranking officer of the JNA who was originally from Bosnia, was appointed to the Chief of General Staff of the Republika Srpska by the leadership of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who appointed him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I want to ask you about one more thing that Candic said. You should know about it. He spoke about a reservist of the JNA by the name of Goran Nikolic. He said that he had liquidated four soldiers, after which, according to Candic, he was only formally arrested and then released. Since this seemed very unlikely to me, I wanted to ask you when you come to testify, is it possible for a soldier to liquidate another soldier in the JNA and then be formally arrested before being released altogether? Do you know anything at all about this event?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know about one case. Goran Nikolic -- I don't know about Goran Nikolic liquidating four soldiers. I know that he liquidated four prisoners from the National Guards Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The ZNG.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But after that, he was taken into custody, interrogated, and a criminal report was filed against him and he was turned over to the military prosecutor. He spent time in the military prison until the end of the state of immediate threat of war, when he was turned over to the civilian prosecution organs, and I think he was later convicted and sentenced. I don't know what sentence was meted out, exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So that was the point of my question. If somebody committed a crime and then he is arrested and released, the person who released him is an accessory to the crime.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: He was arrested, he spent time in the military prison, turned over to civilian authorities, and convicted.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know about that. I don't know about what happened later because I was pensioned off.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know anything about the Candic's claim that members of the JNA killed an Albanian in the village of Ljubace and, according to information that was made available to me, it was true that this commander of the platoon of the military police was killed at a barricade put up by Muslim extremists, and he intervened then in relation to the disarmament of JNA soldiers who were transporting food. Do you know anything about it?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know even the details. It is true what you said. First soldiers were disarmed and the food they were transporting was taken away, and then the commander of the platoon of the military police intervened, this lieutenant who was an Albanian. He was killed at this barricade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: By whom?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the names of these people from the Patriotic People's League who kept the barricade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So he was killed by the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Captain Karavelic Vahid was their superior. After that, Karavelic was arrested along with another three officers from the headquarters which was then based in Zivinice.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. So we've cleared that up as well. Now, tell me, please, is it true that in the JNA there was never any decision taken to form the army of Republika Srpska or, as they called it, the army of Bosnian Serbs at any level within the JNA? No one ever planned to form an army of Republika Srpska, that was something that the authorities of Republika Srpska did. So my question is: Did anyone in the JNA make any decision on the founding of the army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know that anyone in the JNA undertook anything in that direction. I even know of a conversation recounted by General Adzic upon his return from Skopje at Sarajevo airport. I think the conversation was with Karadzic and Koljevic who inquired about the agreement reached the previous day in Skopje - that is, on the 26th - and that at the time, according to General Adzic's interpretation, they were happy to learn that they would get a state of their own and that the JNA would become their army. And this was referred to, ironically, by General Blagoje Adzic. So I'm saying not only did the JNA not participate in it but it even considered it quite impossible.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. General, you mentioned a meeting in my offices in March 1992. I personally do not have as good a memory as you, but as far as I can remember, Zoran Janackovic, that you mentioned, asked me to Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. receive you because you had information that you wished to pass on to me. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say who suggested it. I described how I came to see you. So I was told by Zoran Janackovic. I said literally what he said. "The boss wants to see you." What preceded that, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What preceded it was that he explained to me that you had some information that you wanted to convey to me. Is it true that I didn't ask you anything? I said, "I'm listening to you, please go ahead, General. Tell me what you have to say."

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, Zoran Janackovic in those days was not head of the state security service.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm not saying that. He was in the Ministry of Foreign Affairs.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was going to say that I couldn't -- I didn't communicate with him in those days, nor could I let him know that I had certain information. I described how the conversation went, and it is true that at the time you said you had nothing to ask me because my report was exhaustive.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So I was listening to what you had to say; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that you spoke to me about the influence of the foreign factor and about future demonstrations that were due to be held in March that had been planned for the 9th of March, 1992? And is it true that the foreign factor was behind the first and the subsequent demonstrations, according to the information that you had?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot recall clearly all the things I briefed you about, but it is certain that I spoke about the activities of the foreign factor, and it is quite certain that most of my presentation was devoted to what we had learnt through the military service as to how the demonstrations would develop. Because you know well that both I and General Blagoje Adzic had contacts in February with Vuk Draskovic precisely in order to caution him not to provoke a civil war in the streets in Belgrade through destructive demonstrations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Let's leave aside for a moment the information you provided me with on that occasion. My question is: Do you know that the foreign factor was behind those demonstrations of the 9th of March as well as those of 1991 and 1992?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You see, all the leading opposition figures had numerous contacts with various foreign representatives. I cannot now give you a precise judgement and say that such-and-such a service had given them orders to organise the demonstrations, but it is without any doubt that they were in contact with various foreign representatives, diplomatic representatives and others.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Let's not insist further, as you obviously don't wish to go into any details about that, but did I ask you for any kind of information about generals or any specific information about the army? Did I ask you to inform me further about any details regarding the army?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. You didn't make any specific inquiries about the subjects you have just listed. You just said that you were aware that I was preparing information in the administration and that you would like to see them, that is, reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: As far as I remember, you said that you assumed that I was receiving reports coming from your service and that I said that I was not receiving any reports from your service and that probably there must be some kind of a -- I don't know how to put it. Some kind of filter that is preventing those information -- that information from reaching me. Is that right or not?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's not right. I answered that I was filing reports to the MUP of Serbia, to the MUP of Montenegro, and the federal MUP on a daily basis, and you said that you were receiving some of that but that you were not sure whether some things were concealed from you from time to time, and that is why you would like me to supply you with those reports. I said that if you don't receive the report on the 1st of May, on a state holiday, it means they had been removed and concealed from you, because we were preparing those reports on a daily basis and forwarding them on a daily basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Were you ever present when I called in any general for a conversation? Do you know that I called any general to talk to me from the JNA or the army of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that. I do know what General Adzic told me when I reported to him that I was going to have a talk with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what did General Adzic say?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He said, and I quote, "Thank you for telling me that, but I do know that Slobodan is calling them in, and I'm sure that you will be the first and the last to inform me about it."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So no one had told him that, because he assumed that I was calling people in.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he said he didn't assume, he said he knew.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Let's clear up this matter with Bozidar Stevanovic.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That part was in private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Shall I leave it out or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll go into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: General, let's go back to Kosovo now but not from the point of view of the questions we dealt with straight away but from a general point of view, rather. Is it correct that in Kosovo we had terrorism, not only terrorism of the KLA but many other terrorist organisations, and that in 1999, that is to say at the time when you were reactivated, the army in Kosovo was faced with well-organised terrorist units? Of course not only them, but they also had to face the NATO aggression that was taking place parallelly.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had information from contacts with some persons who were familiar with the situation in Kosovo. As far as back as 1997, objectively speaking, a paramilitary had been established there practically throughout the territory of Kosovo and Metohija and that these were strong and well-armed forces. I also knew of some officers who had previously been in the JNA, and who had been tried for organised hostile activities, to have been heading this paramilitary organisation. That is what I know. I also know that there were other groups, armed groups, smaller groups at the time when I was reactivated and that the blocking Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. and the removal of these groups was primarily under the MUP of Serbia. At the time I went to Kosovo, that's the way it was. And I know there was a dispute -- well, not a dispute, but at this meeting on the 17th of May at your office, you mentioned the spokesperson of the army of Yugoslavia. You said that unconsciously, unnecessarily he made statements to the public that all groups in Kosovo were more or less destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Which was not correct.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was not correct. And secondly, that that could have a detrimental effect, because it could mean that now the army could withdraw and NATO could enter Kosovo because there were no such groups and, therefore, what was the army doing in Kosovo? So I'm just confirming in broad terms what you said just now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. In view of the fact that until 1992 you were uninterruptedly in active service and for a while you were head of the security administration, do you know, according to the information that you had in general regarding the situation in Kosovo, how many citizens of Serb ethnicity during those two decades - let's take these two decades while you were in very active military service - how many had to leave Kosovo because of the pressure that was brought to bear upon them by Albanian extremists?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not have the exact figures. I don't even have tentative figures as to how many Serbs had left Kosovo. But in that period from 1981 when we had to follow the activity of the extreme forces in Kosovo, as it were, there were many examples of pressures of different kinds; rapes, beatings, of Serbs, that is, pressures to have them sell their land and that they move out. So it is evident that part of the extremists in Kosovo did bear -- did exert such pressure. Therefore, in that period it was not even simple to get permission to move out from Kosovo from the authorities. The Serbs wanted to leave Kosovo in big waves, but before they would leave, they would have to get permission from the local authorities stating that they really had a reason to leave, because there was this danger that Kosovo would become ethnically pure. I don't have the actual figures.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: This period that you're talking about from 1980 to 1990, say from 1980 until 1992, while you were still in active military service, was there any pressure exerted by the Serbs against the Albanians, or was this only one-way pressure of the Albanian extremists against the Serbs for the Serbs to move out?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, a minority could not exert that kind of pressure. But among the Serbs, there was a smaller extremist group. You know about it. You know who these people are.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Who? Who are you referring to? I don't know.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For example, Kecmanovic, Bulatovic, and others from Kosovo Polje.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did they kill someone?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me just say what I'm saying. I did not say that they killed anybody, and that's not the question. They were actually heating up things, they were trying to make people resist this. I'm not denying that there were problems, but in the Serb establishment there was also this extremist part that had some very radical extremist views.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Wait a minute. For example, Bulatovic's positions, why would they be extremist if we stated just a minute ago that the Serbs were victims of pressure? Extremist positions are protests against such pressures, and that this protest is exclusively verbal. It did not resort to violence at all. Is that right or is that not right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did they carry out any kind of violence?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They could not apply any violence. But you remember the transports and the trains that were organised from Kosovo that came to Belgrade in order to exert pressure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: For them to protect themselves.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, to redefine the position of Serbs in Kosovo and the relations there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So there was this manipulation that was carried out. People were manipulated and solutions were sought in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now, if we were to go 12 years back, the Serbs would probably wish for the situation that existed in 1990 rather than the situation that they have now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, you know who broke up Yugoslavia and who occupied Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know which Yugoslavia you're referring to. There are several Yugoslavias.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, and also --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We're now moving into general argument. Have you got any other questions about the activities of the Serbs in Kosovo? That was the topic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I am trying to link certain things up.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that after Kosovo, most of the Serbs, before the conflicts broke out in the former SFRY, precisely due to various pressures, were leaving the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina? Before this broke out.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Also the territory of Croatia. Do you know, before the conflicts broke out, how many Serb refugees were coming in from Croatia, coming to Serbia, for example? Did you have any information about that?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are different time periods. I know about the number of the members of the JNA who with their families had left the territory of Slovenia and Croatia. That was about 18.500 people, and about 5.000 families. The fact remains that wherever there were crises or wherever a war broke out, the population migrated accordingly. Not only Serbs. Muslims and Croats were also fleeing from Bosnia-Herzegovina, those who didn't want to take part in these events. This migration, if I can call it that, was particularly characteristic starting February, March 1992, after the first roadblocks were set up in Sarajevo, after the killing of Garudasevic at the Serb wedding there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What happened? Was this the first killing?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is usually considered to be the first killing. However, before that, we already mentioned that officers had been killed, junior officers, non-commissioned officers of the JNA. Ceh Vojko was killed near Listica as far back as August 1991. And then Mihajlovic, another NCO, was killed in the village of Sapna between Tuzla and Zvornik. However, they are not considered to be casualties, victims. It is always Garudasevic who is referred to as the first victim.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The civilian victim, the first civilian victim.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's not put that way. It's always said that the first Serb who was killed was Garudasevic, whereas Sergeant Mihajlovic was also a Serb. So these killings started from the month of August from the area of Western Herzegovina, and then this other case in Tuzla, and then a lieutenant, an Albanian, was killed also in the area near Tuzla by the warehouse of Ljubace between Tuzla and Zivinice, so there were military personnel who were victims before that. But the killing of Garudasevic caused the blocking of Sarajevo that was organised by the SDS. But other parties straight away as well, that is to say the SDA and the HDZ, there were 19 roadblocks on the 1st of March. 12 roadblocks were held by the Serbs, four were held by Muslims, and three were held by Croats. That is when the MUP of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the JNA, in a joint action, removed these roadblocks, and then Sarajevo calmed down on that 1st of March.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. General, can it be said that over these many years there was an explosion of Islamic fundamentalism that had primarily turned itself against the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you know what? These are global assessments, and I prefer dealing with facts. I would rather talk about the spectre of ethnic passions that was fanned in all environments. And instead of being stopped by an organised political action of all the factors that were in a position to do so, objectively speaking, this was fanned. And it was always the other ethnic group that was blamed for something that had been done, whereas one's own people were, in the interpretation of those leaders, victims. The so-called travelling circus, the meetings of the Presidency of Yugoslavia that were having meetings all over the place, saying that they were trying to save Yugoslavia, unfortunately, this proved to be an exercise in futility.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that this confrontation and this instigation of Islamic fundamentalism, this reinstatement of ideas from the Second World War, that this was part of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. You have not been paying attention to his answer. His answer was quite plain, that did he not wish to deal with matters in this way. So to try and put words in his mouth is not a proper way of cross-examining. We will adjourn now. Twenty minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Before I move on with my questions from where I stopped, since we said that the general would read this document which is called "Outline for the presentation of the head of the security administration at the General Staff on the 5th of August, 1991," did you manage to read it?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Just give me a brief answer: Is there anything that you're contesting in this outline or not?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, what is being contested is that it is not a presentation of the General Staff, as it says here, at the General Staff -- or, rather, the staff of the Supreme Command. This is the first thing that is incorrect. This is the monthly report at -- presentation at the staff, and this is rarely attended by the chief of the security administration. One of the heads of divisions within the security administration goes there, either the first or the second. This is done by one of the officials, the clerks there, and it was prepared for one of his superiors. And this is rather partial preparation. I'm sure that that chief did not present things this way. So there are controversial parts. There are statements that should not be made by any means. For example, on page 3. The announcement of the European peacekeepers who had come to Yugoslavia without any opposition of the federal authorities, even the federal Secretary for National Defence. Then it says in parentheses, "In his interviews, the Federal Secretary for National Defence several times pointed out that any crossing of the Yugoslav border of foreign troops in any capacity," et cetera, et cetera, et cetera. So absolutely this is in contrast to the actual relations existing in the General Staff and the authority that General Kadijevic had. No officer could present this kind of assessment, criticise his Federal Secretary. I'm not saying that this is not an authentic paper. I am not saying that this was rigged or anything, but at any rate, this is a clerk who saw things this way and who thought that his chief was supposed to make this kind of presentation. So what is correct, in my opinion, what are the assessments that are correct? That's on page 3, the situation in Croatia. That's what it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, that's what I quoted to you.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. These assessments are correct. Then on page 4, what is absolutely unacceptable is this assessment, that somebody, anybody of responsibility from the administration to have said this. Now I'm quoting: "In this way, the leadership of Croatia is forging its ranks, and at the same time, they are importing high-quality weapons, and they are not going to hesitate to attack all JNA facilities, including the building of the Federal Secretariat of National Defence." I cannot say anything else but that I find this kind of assessment ridiculous, because first of all at that time in that period there were no arms imports. Channels were severed for the most part, and they certainly could not have any weapons in Zagreb that could target Belgrade. There is another thing that is correct, though, in the next paragraph, that there are Howitzers, 122 millimetres and 152 millimetres, but it is also correct that they were working on the procurement of anti-armour missiles and anti-aircraft missiles. These were Stingers and other missiles. Another thing is correct -- I mean, the entire following paragraph is correct. Not to go into all the details, but on page 5, the penultimate paragraph which refers to paramilitary organisation in Kosovo and Metohija, that it was completed, that in this province there is about 400.000 military conscripts who are not deployed, et cetera, et cetera, and that they are working on anti-tank barriers. I can't remember that. And now as for the substance of page 6, that is correct, especially the third part pertaining to the situation in the JNA. I think that that is right. So, Your Honours, this is some kind of a working version of a working paper compiled by one of the clerks at the security administration for speaking at the operative centre of the General Staff but not speaking to the Federal Secretary or the actual General Staff. So I'm sure that I did not attend that presentation, because as chief of the security administration, I very rarely went to the operative centre of the General Staff for presenting a report there because I was subordinated to the Federal Secretary himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. I believe that this is sufficient, but it is not in dispute that what I quoted to you, that is to say attacks against JNA units by the MUP and the ZNG, that this is something that was ongoing and that this is a material truth that you can confirm regardless of whether this was your very own presentation or the presentation of one of your subordinate officers.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the military terminology, in the security administration, we did not use terms like foul attacks. This was a service -- this was an army of Yugoslavia, and every attack against us was foul. It is an adjective that was not customary in the terminology of the security administration. It is enough to say attacks on the JNA, whether they were foul or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You said yourself every attack is foul.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, when we are talking about a legitimate force.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Let us go back to where we left off. We were talking about this activity in Bosnia, in Kosovo, aimed at breaking up Yugoslavia, about terrorism, about the year 1999 and the existence of the terrorist organisation, conflicts with the army, the police, et cetera. Is it true then, according to your own assessment and from what the events -- from the events and the information at your disposal, that attacks by NATO in Kosovo were in open support to Albanian terrorists in their struggle against Yugoslavia and the legal authorities in Yugoslavia, in Serbia?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again this is a global assessment. Whether this was a form of support, it is certain that these forces used it as a form of support to them. But whether this entire aggression was aimed at supporting them or at stopping the conflict in Kosovo, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Before the aggression of NATO in Kosovo, was there any large movement of population from Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose not, but I'm not sure. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, is it true that in certain media and in certain public Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. statements monstrous crimes were mentioned allegedly committed by the army of Yugoslavia in Kosovo and that it was precisely your service which verified the authenticity of such reports and the measure in which they were true? Was that accurate or was this sensationalism?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can speak about only one case involving a journalist from Kraljevo who gave foreign media an article talking about heinous crimes allegedly committed by members of the army of Yugoslavia such as a case when fire was opened from an anti-aircraft machine-gun into the head of a child at a distance of only a couple of metres. All these allegations were checked, and during the investigation, the process of verification, he was not able to quote a single piece of information which would confirm that something like that actually happened. It turned out that he had heard about this in various cafes and taverns from former reservists who recounted these events. Our own attempts to verify it on the ground failed to confirm the writings of this journalist on any point, and he was tried in Nis for spreading false rumours. So this is one case I know about. We verified it and nothing turned out to be true. And he justified himself, saying that he was duped by stories, and he couldn't even name the persons he heard it from.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Okay, General. Before you gave your statement to the investigators, is it true that you were called several times by Natasa Kandic at your home from the so-called front for humanitarian -- human rights?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not several times that she called me. I think it was only once or twice at most. I gave an interview to her on Studio B television where we -- where we marked the anniversary of sufferings in Srebrenica. And she was trying to find out what had happened in Kosovo according to my knowledge. I refused, and I said that there are organs to which I would tell what I know, and I meant precisely this Tribunal. I refused to talk to her, and she did not pester me any further, nor did she call again.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So is this the person who placed in Yugoslav and foreign media the information about the so-called Horseshoe action against Albanians?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you hear about this story about the Horseshoe Operation which was meant to expel Albanians from Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was asked whether I knew about this term, and I said I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know anything at all that would point to the existence of a plan at any level at all in the line of command aimed at expelling Albanians from Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the period when I was actively serving, I don't know of any such plan, but it is a fact that many people left the area. And I believe that in the first part of my testimony, I recounted exactly what I knew about how this area of Kosovo looked like. Apart from large urban areas, everything was completely empty. Under what conditions people had left, I don't know. I assume that a certain part of them left fleeing the war, but based on the examples I quoted regarding certain places, it is obvious that some people left as a consequence of the conduct of certain groups in this area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Can you name at least one unit or a single commander in the army who acted in such a way or issued any orders to that effect, meaning that Albanians should be expelled?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know of any such thing, but if I knew, I would certainly be tried, I would be brought to justice.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you would be tried. During the NATO aggression in 1999, you occupied one of the highest posts in this security administration, the military security administration. Is my assumption true that you did not receive daily reports from every army, considering the fact that communications were often interrupted and there were delays in receipt of information?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is true that we did not receive daily reports from every subordinate group, but we did reports every day. Not from every group, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was it possible then that even the Chief of Staff of the Supreme Command did not have a daily inflow of information about developments in Kosovo for that day, because Kosovo was the area in the greatest danger at the time?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Chief of Staff of the general -- of the Supreme Command could not have data on all developments and all details in Kosovo, because his post was too high. But he did get an operative report every day, because through electronic communications, subordinate commands made available to the operations centre their daily reports summarising the situation on the battlefield for that day, and every Chief of Staff had the daily report of the operation centre. So it's only a question of volume and contents of that report.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. You talked here about the Joint Command in Kosovo during 1999. Is it true that these meetings represented exclusively a coordination of the work of the competent state authorities and nothing that was supposed to be a command jeopardising the regular chain of command in the army and the Ministry of the Interior?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I attended only one such meeting, let me say. It was a relatively short meeting, and I described it. I also told you about the opinion of the Chief of Staff of the Supreme Command on who was getting more information, the Joint Command or he. I don't want to say any more unless we go into private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: This is not a matter for private session. Kosovo was then under heavy bombing. As you know, 40 per cent of all bombing was concentrated only on the territory of Kosovo, which represents 10 per cent of the territory of Serbia. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that figure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it in dispute that the problems that existed in Kosovo had certainly their military aspect and their security aspect and a political aspect as well and an internal political aspect, a foreign political aspect, a social and economic aspect, as well as major problems in terms of supply, health care? It was a large, complex problem which cannot boil down to the question of military units. It was something that encompassed the entire population of Kosovo and Metohija who lived under conditions of constant bombing and actions by terrorist groups; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Every war imposes numerous problems for the territory concerned. Not only the war in Kosovo, but every other war in every other territory. So basically it is true that war triggers a number of problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What could be more logical than this? Since large problems are concentrated in Kosovo, somebody from the federal government should be seconded to serve there, such as Nikola Sainovic from the federal government, somebody from the republican government, Zoran Andjelkovic who was also Deputy Prime Minister, and they, in communication with all political, military, police, and other factors, gather information about the complexity of problems and together with others take part in the coordination of these activities which are aimed at facilitating life for the population, and on the other hand, they should enable an efficient defence from both aggressors and terrorists. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think it is, for this reason: If it was only a question of gathering information for state structures about the situation in this territory from the angle of the military and political situation, this could be achieved through papers and reports. Second, this meeting which I attended, it was not a discussion of the situation in this territory from this aspect that you are talking about. This meeting heard a report on military activities taking part there, the activities of the MUP for the previous day, and it was a planning of activities for the following day. This group made up a command, and it was not disputable that somebody should handle the coordination between the forces of the army of Yugoslavia and the forces of the MUP, because in the previous period, according to the concept of All People's Defence, we had so-called committees for All People's Defence and social self-protection. They had a similar heterogenous composition and we also had state authorities that coordinated these activities. However, this was something else. This was a dislocated command post, because all these things could have been resolved at the level of the General Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Didn't the General Staff deal with things that related to the line of command in the army and the MUP? Are you saying that the unified line of command and the unified single command was somehow cut off, severed by the activity of this body in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would be simpler to say that the commander of the 3rd Army was in a sandwich of sorts in command terms, that is, between the General Staff to which it was subordinated and the Joint Command to which it was reporting. Therefore, from the documents which I was shown here, indicate that this body was giving advice to its superior, saying that they should change their orders regulating the method of views of the body in order to change the decision made in the Joint Command. So it was an unnatural development in the line of command.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Why it was -- why was it unnatural for somebody who was on the ground, closer to the problems, to advise their superiors, saying that they should change something in their decisions because it was more appropriate to the situation on the ground? Wasn't it usual for the subordinate to have some initiative while nevertheless executing orders of the superior?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Even according to the procedure, the subordinate body had to suggest his opinion to the superior. However, when the orders arrived, and the orders did arrive from the General Staff, then it is no longer subject to discussion or suggestions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What if circumstances change and the subordinate thinks that it is appropriate to suggest a change or an adjustment to the situation on the ground? What if that happens?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The problem is that the circumstances were changed by the Joint Command.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It can't be that the Joint Command changed the circumstances. It is the situation on the ground that changes circumstances. And what is the problem with Pavkovic saying something to the Chief of the General Staff?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We would have to analyse the problem further. But we don't even have this original document based on which Pavkovic was saying that the previous decision should be amended.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What are we talking about then?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We are talking about this: The commander of the 3rd Army was between two commands, and when we are discussing this, we should ask the question why at a meeting of this Joint Command he didn't intervene, in view of the failure to execute orders on resubordination of forces in Kosovo? Because that is the place where this issue should have been resolved.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Why should he have intervened if resubordination was carried out, in fact? Let us clear up one thing. Are we clear about this: The order was for MUP units in the area of combat operations during combat operations should be resubordinated to commands of the army, and that is normal practice. So while combat operations are under way in the area of responsibility of a certain military unit, MUP in units this territory are subordinated to the command of that military unit, regardless of whether it is a brigade, a corps, or any other unit. For the duration of combat operations, they are subordinated. They are not subordinated as the Ministry of the Interior in the part of their activity which concerns the issuing of passports, the regulation of traffic, et cetera. They are only resubordinated in the area of responsibility of the military command responsible for these combat operations. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it isn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Are you saying that MUP units in Kosovo in the area of combat operations at the level of brigades or corps were resubordinated to the military command?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is what it says in the intervention by General Pavkovic, but it seems to me that this dates back to the end of May 1999 when he describes that particular situation to the Chief of Staff and complains to him that the resubordination has not been done because from the MUP of Serbia, such an order did not reach subordinate units, and that is why General Ojdanic intervened with you and complained of this situation. And according to what he told me, you answered that that order had not been issued because of the problems in cooperation between the MUP and the army in Kosovo but, rather, because of the problems with the MUP in Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you're claiming that the MUP and the army did not collaborate adequately pursuant to my order or, rather, the order of the Supreme Command, for MUP units to be resubordinated during combat operations to the commands of the army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have said clearly what is stated in General Pavkovic's intervention with General Ojdanic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. We'll discuss that. General Ojdanic is here. At least he is accessible. I do not know he had a problem of that kind. On the contrary, I thought that they were cooperating quite well on the ground, that he personally didn't have that problem.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The cooperation was not good, because you yourself said that we had to get together and resolve these problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, after you had blamed one another for the problems, I said that you have to deal with those problems and that that kind of relationship was equal to sabotage and that all of have you to work in the interests of the state, that that was your duty, rather than to clash amongst yourselves. That was quite true. So there is no dispute over that.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But -- you said that correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Please let me ask you further --

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Allow me to answer your question. Up until the 9th of June -- July, sorry, it was not possible to convene a meeting with the state security services. So from the 17th of May until the 19th of July, the chief of the state security service was not accessible to the chief of the security administration of the army of Yugoslavia, and it was only after General Ojdanic's intervention that the meeting took place on the 9th of July. So problems did exist.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did I order then at that meeting that if there should be any problems I should be informed about them?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether anyone informed you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And the meeting was held upon the intervention of General Ojdanic?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, on the 9th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So when he intervened, the meeting took place. He didn't have to come to me for the meeting to be held.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Chief of General Staff had to intervene, but his -- that is not his level.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I agree, but the meeting was held upon his intervention. Please tell me, could General Pavkovic, as commander of the 3rd Army, regardless of the fact that you will not acknowledge that this was some kind of coordination, could he have acted in any sense outside the orders of the Supreme Staff? Could he have taken any decision? Let us, for instance, say that he's attending this coordination meeting that you call the Joint Command. Could he have taken any decision outside the frameworks of the orders he received from the Supreme Command, and did he make any decision outside the directives of the Supreme Command Staff under the influence of this Joint Command and this same Sainovic that you claim issued orders?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that. I didn't participate, so I cannot give you an answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you don't know whether he took any decision that would be in contrast with the uninterrupted chain of command from the Supreme Command downwards?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I didn't follow the work of the command.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But did you know that Sainovic was vice-president of the federal Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. government?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And that he had been tasked by the Federal Government to be present at Kosovo? Is it logical for the vice-president of the Federal Government to meet with the commander of the 3rd -- with a commander of the corps, the commander of the police, the president of the provisional Executive Council, with other political figures? Don't you find that logical and normal?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's logical.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that same provisional Executive Council of Kosovo and Metohija was composed of Serbs, Albanians, Romanies, Turks, Muslims, Egyptians, that is, representatives of all ethnicities, and that the Serbs were in the minority in that same Executive Council or government? They addressed all problems, ranging from social problems, problems, questions of refugees, electricity supply, medical problems --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You're running on. Quite impossible for the witness to answer. The first question was about the provisional Executive Council and its composition. Do you know about the composition of the Executive Council, General?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am not aware of the composition in concrete terms, but I knew that it was multi-ethnic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So it was multi-ethnic.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You said that Sainovic had certain competencies. You attended that meeting. Was it up to him to approve or order or do anything at that meeting? You yourself said that the atmosphere was informal and that everyone presented his views of their area of responsibility and made their suggestions, each one within their competencies. Pavkovic within the framework of his orders from the Supreme Command, Lukic from the Ministry of the Interior, Sainovic from the federal government, Andjelkovic as president of the provisional Executive Council and member of the republican government. So each one within the framework of his competencies. Was that clear to you or not? You said yourself it was an informal meeting, Sainovic was not issuing any orders. And could Sainovic issue any order to Pavkovic?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again there are many questions in that one question. First, I said and it is a fact that Mr. Sainovic was respected on the basis of the post he had as vice-president of the federal government or as the person sent by you to Kosovo, and without any doubt he had the authority of the most senior person at that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Wasn't he the most senior?
